what_its_for: Labetalol is used to treat high blood pressure (hypertension). Lowering your blood pressure helps prevent strokes, heart attacks, and kidney problems. It works by relaxing your blood vessels and slowing your heart rate so your heart does not have to work as hard.
how_to_take: Take labetalol by mouth with or without food, but try to take it the same way each time (always with food or always without food). Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water. Do not crush or chew the tablet. Take it at the same time(s) every day to keep a steady level in your body. Do not stop taking this medicine suddenly without talking to your doctor first, as stopping abruptly can cause serious heart problems.
dosing: Your doctor will start you on a low dose and slowly increase it based on how your blood pressure responds. A common starting dose is 100 mg taken twice a day (morning and evening). Your doctor may increase your dose over time, up to a maximum of 2,400 mg per day in divided doses. Always follow the exact dose your doctor prescribes — do not change it on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and just take your next regular dose. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store labetalol tablets at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medications out of reach of children and pets. Do not use after the expiration date printed on the label.
what_to_avoid: Avoid standing up too quickly from a sitting or lying position, as labetalol can cause dizziness or lightheadedness, especially when you first start taking it. Avoid drinking alcohol, as it can increase dizziness and lower your blood pressure further. Do not take over-the-counter cold, allergy, or diet medications without checking with your pharmacist first, as many of these can raise your blood pressure or interact with labetalol. Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery until you know how this medicine affects you.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: very slow heartbeat (less than 50 beats per minute), severe dizziness or fainting, shortness of breath or difficulty breathing, swelling of your hands, feet, or ankles, sudden weight gain, chest pain, or signs of liver problems such as yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, or severe stomach pain. Also call your doctor if your blood pressure readings are consistently higher than your target range.
when_it_works: You may start to notice a decrease in your blood pressure within 1 to 2 hours after taking your first dose. However, it may take 1 to 2 weeks of regular use to see the full benefit. Keep taking your medication every day as directed, even if you feel fine. High blood pressure often has no symptoms, so do not stop taking it just because you feel well.
special_populations: Older adults (65 years and older): You may be more sensitive to the dizziness and blood pressure-lowering effects of labetalol. Rise slowly from sitting or lying positions to reduce the risk of falls. Pregnant women: Labetalol is sometimes used during pregnancy to treat high blood pressure, but only under close medical supervision. Tell your doctor right away if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Breastfeeding mothers: Small amounts of labetalol may pass into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Patients with asthma or breathing problems: Labetalol may worsen breathing problems. Tell your doctor if you have asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), or any other lung condition. Patients with diabetes: Labetalol may hide some signs of low blood sugar (such as a fast heartbeat). Monitor your blood sugar closely and report any unusual symptoms to your doctor.
